At the bridal shop in Sibiu
May. Giulia, Ilinca and Doina walk into a bridal shop in Sibiu. Ilinca translates.
So, which one do you like? This white one with lace or that ivory one?
That one over there, by the window. But look at the price! It costs more than three months of my salary.
These are pretty, but they're not mine. Do you understand? I don't feel like myself.
Mum says her wedding dress belonged to her aunt. Could yours belong to someone in the family too?
I've thought about it. Grandma Assunta still has her mother's, from 1930. But it's tiny and ninety years old!
Giulia… you're a restorer. And your grandmother was a seamstress.
(stops) You're right. Why buy a new dress when I can restore ours?
And Matei? What suit will he wear?
He wanted to buy a new one, but your father offered him his own, the one from his wedding.
The one from 1993? It's blue, with enormous shoulders! My boyfriend would never wear it.
Your boyfriend? Ilinca! I didn't know you had one!
(blushing) Er… That's another story. Let's get back to the dresses, please.
QU = "kw", double LL: KWEL-lo, KWEL-la. Not "kello"!
ZZ = a long "ts": PEET-tso. "Seta" with a single S: SE-ta.
An English word pronounced the Italian way: ZMO-king (S before M sounds like "z").
Stress on "NON": bis-NON-na, with a double N.
When they replace a noun, QUESTO and QUELLO agree with it. Careful: QUELLO as a pronoun has only four simple forms — it doesn't change like the article (quel, quegli, quell'…).
Which dress do you prefer? — That one.
Adjective: "quegli stivali", "quel vestito". Pronoun: "quelli", "quello". Not "Prendo quel" or "Prendo quegli"!
To specify distance: "questo qui" (this one here), "quello lì / là" (that one there).
The possessive can stand alone, with the article, so you don't repeat the noun. The form is the same as the adjective:
Il mio vestito è vecchio, il tuo è nuovo.
La sua famiglia è grande, la nostra è piccola.
I miei genitori vengono. E i tuoi?
My parents are coming. And yours?
Le loro case sono vicine alle nostre.
Their houses are close to ours.
As in Romanian: "al meu, a ta, ai noștri". Except that Italian uses the definite article (il, la, i, le) instead of "al / a / ai / ale".
After ESSERE, when you just say whose something is, the article is usually dropped:
Questo libro è il mio, non il tuo.
Di chi è la borsa? — È sua.
Quale borsa è la sua? — La sua è quella rossa.
Set expressions: "I miei" = my parents (Vado dai miei = I'm going to my parents'). "Alla nostra!" = To us! (a toast)

Quello del matrimonio di suo padre

The parcel from Naples arrived in Sibiu one May morning. It was enormous, wrapped in three layers of paper and tied with string, the way things used to be done. On top, in Assunta's shaky handwriting, it said: "FRAGILE. IT WAS MY MOTHER'S. AND NOW IT'S YOURS."

Giulia opened it on the kitchen table, her hands trembling. Inside, among sheets of yellowed tissue paper, was the dress: ivory silk, a long lace veil, little mother-of-pearl buttons. It smelled of lavender and old wardrobes.

Doina came closer and touched the lace with two fingers, the way you touch something sacred. She said something in Romanian. "She says it's more beautiful than hers," Matei translated. "And that hers was already very beautiful."
But there were problems. Giulia's great-grandmother had been a tiny woman: the dress was tight and short. In some places the silk was damaged. The veil had three holes, and a button was missing.

That evening Giulia phoned her grandmother. "Grandma, the dress is gorgeous, but it's small. Can I alter it?" Assunta laughed. "The dress is yours, my girl. It's not mine any more, and it's not my mother's any more. Do what you like with it. I let it out myself in 1954, for my wedding, and my mother said nothing."

"This isn't a dress," Giulia said, her eyes shining. "This is a restoration." And for three weeks, every evening after work at the museum, she and Matei worked on the dress as if it were a fifteenth-century painting: with patience, magnifying glasses and tweezers.

To let it out they asked for help from a Sibiu seamstress, Mrs Elena, who was seventy-eight and had golden hands. She found an almost identical silk in a shop in the old town. "This one is perfect," she said. "The one in the shop next door is more expensive, but less beautiful."

The missing button was the hardest problem. There were no matching ones left anywhere. Then Doina opened a tin box she had kept in her wardrobe for thirty years. Inside were the buttons from her own wedding dress. One was almost identical to the Neapolitan great-grandmother's.
"Take mine," said Doina, putting it in Giulia's hand. Matei didn't need to translate: Giulia had understood. So now, on the 1930 Neapolitan dress, there was a 1993 Romanian button.

And Matei's suit? Ion had taken it out of the wardrobe: blue, enormous, with square shoulders and very wide trousers. Matei tried it on in front of the mirror and looked at his father. "Dad, yours is… very nineties." Ion laughed for the first time all week. "And your outfit at Giulia's party was very dirty," he replied. Someone had obviously told him about the dog.

In the end Mrs Elena took in Ion's suit too. At the final fitting Giulia came out of the room in her great-grandmother's dress, with the mended veil and Doina's button. Nobody spoke. Doina was crying. Ion was looking at the floor. Matei, who had seen a thousand masterpieces, thought it was the most beautiful restoration of his life. Ilinca took a photo and sent it to Naples. Assunta's reply came a minute later: "Now it's truly yours."
